slides.title: Chapter 13: Bitcoin Security
slides.sub: How keys are protected, backed up, shared and handed on, and what each safeguard costs

items.body: Picture: the Bitcoin logo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Python 3.14.6; Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are recorded from one run, not run here.

slides.notes: This deck explains how Bitcoin coins are kept safe: what a signature protects, where keys are stored, how they are backed up and shared, and what an heir needs. Every number on a result picture was computed, or read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core 31.1 on a test network.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Six parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has six parts that follow the order of the chapter. Four true stories and twenty-eight code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.take: Six parts, twenty-eight examples, four true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: Why can a signed payment be published without showing the key, and what breaks it?
What does a node trust, and how can it check the first block and a download?
How do cold storage, a locked wallet and a signing device each protect keys?
What does a backup or a set of seed words restore, and what does it miss?
What do several keys and shared secrets buy, and what do they cost?
What does it mean to leave your coins with an exchange?
How can an heir be allowed to spend after a wait, and what was not run here?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.title: One chapter, six parts
slides.sub: The concept map the whole deck hangs on
slides.notes: The chapter has six parts and 25 key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with everyday comparisons, code that runs, and some parts a true story. The deck follows the order of the chapter.
slides.take: Six parts; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: The security model
slides.sub: A node trusts only what it can check itself, like a cashier who tests every note.

items.meaning: A signed payment can be published because it never contains the key.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque that shows the signature but never the pen.

items.meaning: Nodes talk in an encrypted language by default; old nodes fall back.
items.analogy: Think of two people who switch to a private language.

items.meaning: One typed-in block is the start of all checking.
items.analogy: Think of the founder at the top of a family tree.

items.meaning: A hash proves the download is the listed file; a signature says who listed it.
items.analogy: Think of a seal on a medicine box.

slides.notes: A node trusts only what it can check. This part shows why a signed payment can be published, how peers talk, where checking starts, and what a download proves.

slides.title: The security model: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Bitcoin Security
items.meaning: Keeping coins safe by keeping the keys safe, and by checking what you run.
items.analogy: Think of locking your front door and also checking who made the lock.

items.label: Security Principles
items.meaning: Rules such as trusting as little as possible and checking what you can.
items.analogy: Think of the habits of a cashier who tests every note.

items.label: Developing Bitcoin Systems Securely
items.meaning: Builders must assume attackers read the code and copy the data.
items.analogy: Think of building a shop on the assumption that burglars know the plan.

items.label: The Root of Trust
items.meaning: The book's name for the one thing a system must simply believe.
items.analogy: Think of the founder at the top of a family tree.

slides.notes: These cards cover Bitcoin Security, Security Principles, Developing Bitcoin Systems Securely and The Root of Trust. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 13.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A signed payment hides the key
slides.sub: What the recorded bytes of a payment contain

groups.note: The recorded signed payment of the test node, as bytes.
Its witness holds a signature and a public key, never the key itself.
Neither the raw key nor its wallet export form appears in the bytes.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: what the signed bytes contain
The witness holds a signature of 71 bytes and a public key of 33 bytes. No key of the owner is in the payment.

slides.notes: A payment can be published because it contains a signature and a public key, not the private key. The recorded bytes of one signed payment show the witness items and their sizes, and no key of the owner. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The payment carries a signature and a public key, never the private key

slides.title: The security model: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: root of trust
items.meaning: Everything checked later is checked against this starting point.
items.analogy: Think of the zero mark on a ruler.

items.label: decentralization
items.meaning: No single party can change or stop the system.
items.analogy: Think of a town square with no single owner.

items.label: decentralized consensus
items.meaning: Thousands of nodes check the same rules and so agree on one history.
items.analogy: Think of a class where every pupil marks the same sum.

items.label: genesis block
items.meaning: The first block, whose hash is typed into the software.
items.analogy: Think of the first page of a ledger, signed in advance.

slides.notes: These cards cover root of trust, decentralization, decentralized consensus and genesis block. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 13.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Edit the payee or the amount: rejected
slides.sub: The node tested the payment as signed and two edited copies

groups.note: The node was offered the payment as signed and two edited copies.
Only the copy that was signed is allowed into the mempool.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: three copies offered to the node
Both edited copies really differ from the original (yes), and both are refused: the signature covered what was changed.

slides.notes: The signature covers the amounts and the receiving scripts. A copy with another payee, or another amount, is no longer what was signed, so the node refuses it. Only the original is allowed. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A signature covers payee and amount, so any edit fails the check

slides.title: A replayed payment pays nothing
slides.sub: Offering a mined payment to the same node again

groups.note: A mined payment is offered to the same node a second time.
The receiver's balance before and after the replay is compared.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: the replay and its effect
A node that already knows a payment will not take it again: nothing is paid twice.

slides.notes: Sending the same signed payment again gains nothing. The node already knows it and says so, and the receiver's balance does not change. A signature is not a bearer cheque that can be cashed twice. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A node that knows a payment refuses it, so nothing is paid twice

slides.title: Encrypted by default since release 27.0
slides.sub: Two recorded nodes, and one without the service

groups.note: Two recorded nodes both speak the new encrypted transport.
Both ends of the link derived the same session identifier.
A node without the service falls back to the old version one.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: who speaks which version
Both ends of an encrypted link derive the same session identifier. The node without the service stays on version one.

slides.notes: Since release 27.0 nodes talk over the encrypted transport of BIP 324. Two recorded peers both report version two and the same session identifier. A node without the service falls back to the plain version one. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Peers with the service speak version two; others stay on version one

slides.title: The first block's hash, rebuilt
slides.sub: Eighty bytes, hashed twice, found in the source

groups.note: The Merkle root of the first block, as printed in explorers.
The 80-byte header: version, parent, root, time, bits, nonce.
Hash it twice and look the result up in the source of Core.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; seen() searches a saved source

items.body: Result: the double hash of the header
The hash begins with 10 zero digits and appears in the source of Core: the starting point is typed in.

slides.notes: The header of the first block has 80 bytes. Hashing it twice gives the hash that Bitcoin Core carries in its source. Software checks every later block against this typed-in starting point. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The first block is not fetched; its hash is typed into the software

slides.title: Assumed valid: a typed-in shortcut
slides.sub: Where Core describes it and where it keeps the block

groups.note: The help text of release 31.1 describes the shortcut in words.
The block it trusts is typed into the source, like the genesis block.
An option of the recorded node controls it.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; seen() searches a saved source

items.body: Result: three searches in saved sources
The shortcut is documented, typed into the release and switchable. Trust in it is trust in the release.

slides.notes: To start faster, a node may skip checking old signatures for blocks that lead up to a block hash typed into the release. The help text describes it, the source holds the hash, and an option controls it. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Old blocks are trusted by a block hash typed into the release

slides.title: Does the download match the list?
slides.sub: The recorded check of the release 31.1 tarball

groups.note: The recorded download of Bitcoin Core 31.1 and its hash list.
The list names every file; the tarball hash is one line of it.
Builders signed the list, but without their keys none could be checked.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: the recorded download check
The hash proves the file is the listed one. Without the builders' keys, nothing says who made the list.

slides.notes: The hash of the downloaded file equals its line in the signed list. That proves the file is the listed one. Eleven builders signed the list, but their keys were not imported, so no signature was checked. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A matching hash proves the file; a checked signature proves who listed it

slides.title: Protecting keys
slides.sub: Keys are kept where thieves cannot reach, like cash in a safe and not in a pocket.

items.meaning: Keys stay on a machine that is never online; only the signed file travels.
items.analogy: Think of a manager who signs cheques in another building.

items.meaning: A passphrase locks the keys but not the balance.
items.analogy: Think of a locked drawer in a shop window.

items.meaning: A small device holds the keys and signs, and waits longer after each wrong PIN.
items.analogy: Think of a safe that empties itself after too many tries.

items.meaning: Paper wallets are obsolete; a secret made of a few words is quickly guessed.
items.analogy: Think of a password written on a sticky note.

slides.notes: Coins are as safe as their keys. We compare a watching wallet with a signing one, see a device that makes a thief wait, and count what a guess costs.

slides.title: Protecting keys: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: User Security Best Practices
items.meaning: The book's advice for people who hold keys.
items.analogy: Think of the safety rules printed on a ladder.

items.label: best practices
items.meaning: Habits that experience shows to work, such as offline keys and tested backups.
items.analogy: Think of washing your hands before cooking.

items.label: Physical Bitcoin Storage
items.meaning: Keeping the secret on paper, metal or a device that can be locked away.
items.analogy: Think of keeping a spare key in a bank box.

slides.notes: These cards cover User Security Best Practices, best practices and Physical Bitcoin Storage. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 13.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A watch-only wallet cannot sign
slides.sub: The online half of cold storage

groups.note: The recorded online wallet that only watches the coins.
Asked to sign a payment, it cannot finish the job.
Asked for private descriptors, it answers with a refusal text.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: the online wallet of cold storage
Asked for private descriptors it answers: Can't get private descriptor string for. It can watch and build, never sign.

slides.notes: The online wallet holds only public information. It sees the balance and builds a payment, but it cannot sign, and it refuses to list private descriptors. That is why a thief of this machine gets no coins. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A wallet without keys can build payments but never finish them

slides.title: Protecting keys: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Hardware Signing Devices
items.meaning: Small devices that hold the keys and sign inside.
items.analogy: Think of a safe that makes you wait longer after each wrong code.

items.label: cold storage
items.meaning: Keys on a machine that is never connected to the network.
items.analogy: Think of cash in a safe at home, not in your pocket.

items.label: paper backup
items.meaning: The seed written on paper; fine for a copy, poor for daily use.
items.analogy: Think of a recipe card kept in the kitchen drawer.

slides.notes: These cards cover Hardware Signing Devices, cold storage and paper backup. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 13.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The payment file travels offline and back
slides.sub: A partially signed payment goes to the cold node

groups.note: The cold node has no blocks and no network connection.
It signs the file and returns a longer one.
The online node finishes it and the payment confirms.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: characters of the payment file, before and after signing
The cold node, with 0 blocks and 0 connections, signed it. The online node finished it: 1 confirmation, 1.0 coin received.

slides.notes: The online wallet writes an unsigned payment file. The cold node, with no blocks and no connection, signs it and returns a longer file. The online node finishes it and the payment confirms. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Only the file travels; the keys never touch the online machine

slides.title: Hot or cold?
slides.sub: Why the keys live on a machine that is never online

left.head: A hot wallet is online
rows: A thief of the machine can reach the keys.
Like the cash in your pocket.

right.head: Cold storage is offline
rows: Only a signed file travels in.
The keys never touch a connected machine.
Like a safe kept at home.

slides.notes: A hot wallet keeps its keys on a machine that is online, so malware or a thief of the machine can reach them. Cold storage keeps them on a machine that is never connected, and only signed files travel.
slides.take: Hot is handy, cold is safe; many people keep both

slides.title: A PIN that makes the thief wait
slides.sub: The waits of a hardware wallet double after each wrong try

rows: wait = [2 ** k for k in range(tries)]
groups.note: After each wrong PIN the wait doubles, starting from one second.
Fifteen waits add up to a number of seconds, and of hours.

rows: q = 'wipe itself after 16 failed PIN entry attempts'
groups.note: The saved wiki page says the device wipes itself after sixteen tries.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; seen() searches a saved source

items.body: Result: seconds waited after each wrong PIN, tries 1 to 15
The waits add up to 32,767 seconds, 9.1 hours. The saved wiki page says the device wipes itself after 16 tries: yes.

slides.notes: A hardware wallet answers wrong PINs with waits that double: 1, 2, 4 seconds and so on. Fifteen waits add up to hours, and after sixteen failed tries the device wipes itself, so guessing is hopeless. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Waiting costs the thief hours long before the device wipes itself

slides.title: The little box that learned to wait
slides.sub: A device that makes a thief wait

items.cap: Trezor Model T - FlippyFlink, CC0 1.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: SatoshiLabs announced the Trezor Safe 5 on 14 June 2024 at BTC Prague, with a colour touchscreen and an EAL 6+ secure element.
WHY: A thief with the device must guess the PIN, and every wrong try costs more waiting.
HOW: The waits double, 1, 2, 4 seconds and so on, and after 16 failed tries the device wipes itself.
SO WHAT: A signing box protects the key; you protect the intent by reading the address on its own screen.

items.body: Stand-in: a Trezor Model T, not the Safe 5.

items.who: SatoshiLabs, the company behind the Trezor hardware wallets, and the people at BTC Prague where the Trezor Safe 5 was announced
items.where: BTC Prague, and the Bitcoin Wiki page on Trezor

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2024-06-14. A Trezor holds the keys and makes the signatures, and defends itself against a thief with a PIN whose waits double, 1 second after the first wrong try, 2 after the second, 4 after the third, and a wipe after 16 failed attempts.

slides.title: Four words fall in seconds
slides.sub: How long a phrase of words lasts against a fast rig

groups.note: A phrase of four words from a list of 2048: how many choices?
Assume a cracking rig that tries a trillion guesses a second.
Seconds needed to try every phrase of that length:

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: time to try every phrase at 10^12 guesses a second
Four words give 17,592,186,044,416 phrases and last 17.6 seconds. Six words last 2.3 years.

slides.notes: A phrase made of words from a list of 2048 has 2048 to the power of its length in possibilities. At a trillion guesses a second four words last seconds, six words about two years. Choose long, random secrets. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A few random words are not a safe secret on their own

slides.title: A locked wallet still shows the balance
slides.sub: A passphrase locks the keys, not the view

groups.note: The recorded wallet after it was encrypted with a passphrase.
Sending is refused with a plain message that names the cure.
A wrong passphrase gives another refusal; unlocking lasts a few seconds.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: the encrypted wallet
Sending is refused with: "Error: Please enter the wallet". The wrong passphrase gives: "The wallet passphrase entered wa"

slides.notes: After encryption the wallet still shows the balance and creates addresses, because those need no private key. Sending is refused until the passphrase is entered, and a wrong passphrase is refused too. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The balance stays visible; spending needs the passphrase

slides.title: Stretching the passphrase buys days
slides.sub: Core repeats a hash thousands of times per guess

groups.note: Bitcoin Core stretches the passphrase; its source names the rounds.
Assume a guessing rig that runs 250,000 rounds a second.
A passphrase worth thirty bits then takes days to exhaust.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L.const reads a constant from a saved source

items.body: Result: the cost of guessing a passphrase
Each guess costs 0.1 seconds on the assumed rig, so thirty bits of passphrase hold out for 1242.8 days.

slides.notes: Bitcoin Core stretches the passphrase by repeating a hash many times, so each guess costs time. We assume a rig and a passphrase of thirty bits of strength, and count the days an attacker needs. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: More rounds per guess mean more days for an attacker

slides.title: Keeping access
slides.sub: Access survives loss through a backup, like a spare key in a drawer.

items.meaning: Twelve words and a checksum stand for all the keys of a wallet.
items.analogy: Think of a recipe card from which the same dish is cooked again.

items.meaning: A backup restores only what it knew when it was made.
items.analogy: Think of a spare key cut before the locksmith adds new locks.

slides.notes: Safe keys are no use if you lose them. We see what a backup restores, how twelve words stand for every key, and where a master key comes from.

slides.title: Keeping access: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Ensuring Your Access
items.meaning: Planning so that you can still reach your coins after a loss.
items.analogy: Think of keeping a copy of your house key with a neighbour.

items.label: backing up
items.meaning: Saving what a wallet needs, and doing it again after changes.
items.analogy: Think of photocopying a document after each new page.

items.label: recovery codes
items.meaning: A short secret that rebuilds the keys, such as the seed words.
items.analogy: Think of the reset code printed in a new phone's box.

items.label: seed
items.meaning: The number from which every key of a wallet is derived.
items.analogy: Think of a single seed that grows into a whole orchard.

slides.notes: These cards cover Ensuring Your Access, backing up, recovery codes and seed. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 13.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A stale backup misses the newest coins
slides.sub: Two restores of the same recorded wallet

groups.note: The recorded wallet held coins; one backup is late, one early.
The early copy knows fewer addresses, so it misses coins.
The late copy also knows an address far ahead in the pool.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: coins found by the wallet and by two restores
The early copy finds 1.0 of 3.0 coins. Address 9, far ahead in the pool, is known to the late copy (yes) and not to the early one.

slides.notes: A wallet pre-computes a pool of addresses. A backup taken early knows few of them. Restoring from it finds fewer coins than the wallet holds, while a late backup finds them all. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A backup restores only what it knew when it was made

slides.title: A backup range covers only the pool
slides.sub: The same idea with whole numbers you can change

groups.note: The backup knows the first three addresses of the key pool.
Two payments arrived: one coin at address 1, two at address 9.

rows: found = sum(c for i, c in paid if i < pool)
total = sum(c for i, c in paid)
groups.note: Only payments to known addresses are found after a restore.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: coins found against coins paid
Only 1 of 3 coins sit at addresses the backup knows. The other coins are on the chain but invisible to the restored wallet.

slides.notes: Change the pool size or the payments and rerun. Only payments sent to addresses inside the backup's pool are found after a restore. The rest are on the chain but invisible to the restored wallet. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Coins sent beyond the known addresses are not found

slides.title: Twelve words, 128 bits and a checksum
slides.sub: The arithmetic of BIP 39

groups.note: Sixteen bytes of entropy are 128 bits; one bit in 32 is a checksum.
Entropy and checksum are cut into groups of eleven bits: one word each.
A wrong word set passes the checksum one time in sixteen.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: how the words are made
12 words carry 128 bits and a 4-bit check; one wrong word set in 16 would pass by luck.

slides.notes: Sixteen bytes of entropy are 128 bits. One bit in 32 is added as a checksum and everything is cut into groups of eleven bits, each choosing one of 2048 words. That gives twelve words. It is example 16 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A wrong word set passes the checksum only one time in sixteen

slides.title: Seed words are stretched into a seed
slides.sub: The first test vector of BIP 39

groups.note: The twelve words of the first official test vector of BIP 39.
Stretching the words with a passphrase gives a 64-byte seed.
The same words with no passphrase give another seed.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the seed from the words
Same words, other passphrase, other seed: the passphrase is part of the secret.

slides.notes: The words are hashed many times, with the passphrase as salt, into a 64-byte seed. We compare it with the official test vector. With no passphrase the same words give a different seed, hence another wallet. It is example 17 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The same words with another passphrase give another wallet

slides.title: A master key grows from the seed
slides.sub: The first test vector of BIP 32

groups.note: The first official test seed of BIP 32 is sixteen bytes.
A keyed hash splits it into a master key and a chain code.
The extended key matches the published test vector.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the master key of the seed
Key and chain code together are the root from which every key of the wallet is derived.

slides.notes: A keyed hash of the seed splits into a master private key and a chain code. All the wallet's keys are derived from this pair. We compare with the published test vector of BIP 32. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Every key of the wallet descends from these two values

slides.title: Sharing control
slides.sub: Control is shared among keys or pieces, like a vault that needs two keyholders.

items.meaning: Two of three keys must sign, so one lost or stolen key is not fatal.
items.analogy: Think of a safe deposit box that needs two keyholders.

items.meaning: A secret is cut into shares; enough of them rebuild it, fewer reveal nothing.
items.analogy: Think of a map torn in three: two pieces show the spot.

slides.notes: One key is one point of failure. Several keys and shared secrets spread loss and theft, and we measure what that costs in bytes and in chances.

slides.title: Sharing control: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Diversifying Risk
items.meaning: Not putting all trust in one key, one place or one person.
items.analogy: Think of not keeping all your eggs in one basket.

items.label: risk diversification
items.meaning: Spreading loss and theft over several keys so that no single failure is fatal.
items.analogy: Think of splitting savings across several banks.

items.label: Multisig and Governance
items.meaning: Several keyholders, such as partners, agree before coins move.
items.analogy: Think of a board of directors that must vote before a payment.

items.label: multisignature addresses
items.meaning: Addresses that need m signatures out of n keys.
items.analogy: Think of a safe deposit box that needs two of three keyholders.

slides.notes: These cards cover Diversifying Risk, risk diversification, Multisig and Governance and multisignature addresses. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 13.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Two of three keys sign
slides.sub: Recorded signing with one, two and three keys

groups.note: One key signs the recorded payment, then a second key joins.

rows: lost = [l[k] for k in sorted(l) if k.startswith('lose')]
groups.note: Lose one key: the other two still sign. Lose two: they do not.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: who can finish the payment
Two of three keys are enough, and one lost key is no disaster. The node accepted the signed payment: yes.

slides.notes: A two-of-three wallet needs two signatures. One key alone leaves the payment unfinished. If one key is lost the other two still sign, but with two keys lost the wallet cannot be spent. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: One key alone cannot sign; any two of the three can

slides.title: More keys: fewer losses, more thefts
slides.sub: Chances of being stuck or robbed

groups.note: Three schemes: one key, two of three, one of three.

rows: lose = lambda m, n: round(L.p_lose(0.1, m, n), 4)
stuck = [lose(m, n) for m, n in schemes]
groups.note: Each key is lost with chance 0.1; the funds are stuck if too few remain.

rows: rob = lambda m, n: round(L.p_theft(0.05, m, n), 5)
robbed = [rob(m, n) for m, n in schemes]
groups.note: Each key is stolen with chance 0.05; a thief needs m of them.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: chance of loss and of theft, per scheme
Two of three cuts both risks against one key. One of three is stuck rarely but robbed 14.26 % of the time.

slides.notes: A scheme that needs fewer keys is easier to use but easier to rob. With a loss chance of 0.1 and a theft chance of 0.05 per key, two of three is the balance; one of three is often robbed. It is example 20 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Two of three cuts both risks; one of three trades loss for theft

slides.title: A two-of-three payment is larger
slides.sub: Virtual bytes of one spend

groups.note: The recorded sizes in virtual bytes of a one-key and a two-of-three spend.
Two signatures out of three keys: m = 2 and n = 3.
Counting the script parts by hand gives the same number.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: virtual bytes of one spend
Counting the script parts by hand gives 146, the same as the node recorded. More signatures mean a higher fee.

slides.notes: A multisignature spend carries several signatures and the script that lists the keys. The recorded sizes in virtual bytes show the cost. Counting the script parts by hand gives the same number. It is example 21 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: Shamir by hand: shares on a line
slides.sub: A line, three points, a secret at zero

groups.note: Work modulo 47 with secret 12 and slope 30: the line is 12 + 30x.

rows: y = [(s + a * x) % p for x in (1, 2, 3)]
groups.note: The shares are the line's heights at x = 1, 2 and 3.
Two shares rebuild the line, and its height at zero is the secret.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: three shares and the secret
Two shares fix the line and give 12, its height at zero. One share alone does not.

slides.notes: The secret is the height of a line at zero, and each share is its height at another point. Two points fix the line, so two shares rebuild the secret. Try other numbers and rerun; this is example 22 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Two points fix the line; its height at zero is the secret

slides.title: Shamir with the chapter library
slides.sub: Three shares, any two rebuild the secret

groups.note: A secret is cut into three shares; the slope is fixed here.
Any two of the three shares rebuild the secret.
One share alone rebuilds a number that is not the secret.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: shares and what they rebuild
The shares are ordinary numbers. Pairs of them agree on 123456789; a single share does not give it.

slides.notes: The library cuts a secret into three shares with a fixed slope so that the run repeats. Any two shares rebuild the secret. A single share rebuilds some number, but not the secret. It is example 23 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: One share alone gives no information about the secret

slides.title: One share fits every secret
slides.sub: A small field where every case can be listed

groups.note: Work modulo 11. A single share has height 5 at x = 1.

rows: fits = {(s, (y - s) % p) for s in range(p)}
(len(fits), len({s for s, a in fits}), p)
groups.note: For every possible secret there is a slope that fits the share.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the slope that fits the share, for each possible secret s
All 11 possible secrets have a slope that fits the one share we hold: it reveals nothing.

slides.notes: In a small field we can list every possibility. For each possible secret exactly one slope fits the single share we hold. So the share alone tells nothing about which secret is the true one. It is example 24 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A single share is consistent with every possible secret

slides.title: Three pieces of a key, any two will do
slides.sub: Shares of a secret: loss and theft both need several failures

items.cap: Adi Shamir Royal Society - Duncan Hull, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: In November 1979 Adi Shamir published How to Share a Secret, two pages in the Communications of the ACM.
WHY: A secret kept in one place is lost or stolen with it; shares make both loss and theft need several failures.
HOW: Any k of n shares rebuild the secret by polynomial interpolation, and k minus 1 shares leave it completely undetermined.
SO WHAT: Codex32 and SLIP39 apply the same idea to seed words.

items.who: Adi Shamir, then at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and co-inventor of RSA, and the editor Rivest of the Communications of the ACM
items.where: the Communications of the ACM, volume 22, number 11, November 1979, pages 612 and 613
items.linkText: Shamir: How to Share a Secret (PDF, 1979)

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 1979-11-01. Adi Shamir's two-page paper How to Share a Secret divides data D into n pieces so that D is easily computable from any k pieces and knowledge of any k minus 1 pieces leaves D completely undetermined. The lesson is that split the secret so that loss and theft both need several failures.

slides.title: Custody history
slides.sub: Handing coins to someone else is trust, like leaving cash with a stranger.

items.meaning: When an exchange holds the keys, customers hold only a claim on it.
items.analogy: Think of leaving your cash with a shopkeeper who may close.

items.meaning: A coin can hide a key under a seal that shows if it was opened.
items.analogy: Think of a tamper seal on a medicine bottle.

slides.notes: Giving your coins to someone else is trust, not safety. Two true stories show what happens when a shop or a seal replaces your own key.

slides.title: The exchange that held the keys of everyone
slides.sub: The coins of everyone sat in one wallet of the exchange

items.cap: Letter regarding Mt.Gox - NetSPI, CC BY 2.0, Flickr

items: WHAT: Mt. Gox of Shibuya, Tokyo, halted withdrawals on 7 February 2014 and suspended all trading on 24 February.
WHY: It kept customers' coins in its own wallets, so customers held a claim on the exchange and not the keys.
HOW: A leaked document said 744,408 coins were stolen unnoticed for years; the Tokyo court found Karpeles guilty of falsifying data.
SO WHAT: Not your keys, not your coins: custody is trust.

items.body: Stand-in: a bankruptcy letter, not the theft.

items.who: Mark Karpeles, who bought the site in March 2011 and ran it as CEO, Jed McCaleb, who founded it
items.where: the exchange Mt. Gox in Shibuya, Tokyo, Japan, and its website mtgox.com

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2014-02-24. Mt. Gox, based in Shibuya, was launched in 2010 and was handling over 70% of all bitcoin transactions worldwide by early 2014. The lesson is that not your keys, not your coins: custody is trust.

slides.title: A coin with a private key under a sticker
slides.sub: A private key hidden under a hologram

items.cap: Casascius hologram close-up - BTC Keychain, CC BY 2.0, Flickr

items: WHAT: Mike Caldwell sold physical bitcoins: a coin with the private key under a hologram that shows a honeycomb pattern when peeled.
WHY: A peeled seal shows that someone looked, which a bare slip of paper cannot do.
HOW: Coins came in 1, 10, 25, 100 and 1000 BTC; FinCEN said minting them made him a money transmitter, so sales stopped on 26 November 2013.
SO WHAT: A tamper seal tells you someone looked, not who.

items.body: Stand-in: a hologram close-up, not the coin.

items.who: Mike Caldwell, the maker of the Casascius coins, and FinCEN
items.where: Sandy, Utah, USA, and the Bitcoin community that bought the coins

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2013-11-26. Mike Caldwell first imagined a private key on a piece of paper inside a washer with a tamper-evident hologram on each side, and found it more economical to make a real coin. The lesson is that a tamper seal tells you someone looked, not who.

slides.title: The heir must wait ten blocks
slides.sub: A recorded timelock: owner at once, heir after a wait

groups.note: The recorded policy: the owner at any time, or the heir after ten blocks.
The heir tried after 1, 9 and 10 confirmations.
The refusal before the time names the rule.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: the recorded timelock tests
The policy is or(owner, and(heir, older 10)). Before the wait the node says: non-BIP68-final.

slides.notes: The policy lets the owner spend at any time and the heir only after ten confirmations. The recorded tests show the heir refused after one and nine confirmations and accepted at ten. It is example 27 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Before the wait, the node refuses the heir's payment

slides.title: The wait field has sixteen bits
slides.sub: A trap in the heir's timelock

groups.note: The wait field of a relative timelock has sixteen bits.
The value 65536 does not fit; its low sixteen bits are zero.
In blocks of ten minutes the longest wait is counted in days.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R is the recorded run of Core 31.1

items.body: Result: the sixteen-bit wait field
A wait of 65536 wraps to 0, so the recorded heir could spend at once: yes.

slides.notes: The relative wait is stored in sixteen bits, so it cannot exceed 65535 blocks, about 455 days. A value of 65536 is cut to zero in those bits, which lets the heir spend at once. Check your own numbers. It is example 28 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A wait of 65536 wraps to zero, so the heir can spend at once

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per idea, each provable from its slides

items: A signed payment shows no key, and editing its payee or amount breaks the signature; peers talk encrypted and trust one typed-in block.
Keys stay offline in cold storage, behind a passphrase, or in a device that waits longer after each wrong PIN.
A backup restores only what it knew; twelve words and a checksum rebuild every key of a wallet.
Two of three keys cut the chance of being stuck but raise the chance of theft; one share of a secret reveals nothing.
An exchange holds claims, not keys; an heir can be made to wait ten blocks; some safeguards were not run here.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature, one for each group of parts. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed or read from the recorded run. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all 28 examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
